newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Thai gov't will support property sector - Amnuay.
newsitem.headline: Thai gov't will support property sector - Amnuay.

text.p: Thailand's government will support the country's troubled property sector, Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said Monday.
"The government will provide stimulus in the property market and liquidity. The central bank has been very active in this area," said Amnuay.
But in supporting the property sector, the government "will not be throwing money around," Amnuay said.
He said that adding liquidity to the property sector did not necessarily mean "supplying cheap funds to financial institutions just because they are in trouble."
Rather, aid to the sector could take other forms, Amnuay said, though he did not elaborate.
Amnuay said he did not foresee weakness in the property sector causing financial institutions to fail, although property developers may be at risk.

He said commercial banks have only modest exposure to the property sector. And while the exposure of the financial institutions is higher, "it is not something that is so serious that it cannot be overcome," he said.
Amnuay said Thailand's fundamentals remain strong but the country still requires measures to correct short-term imbalances in the economy.
"I believe fundamentals of the economy are still strong," he said. "But we still want to re-balance our policymaking to stabilise the economy."
He said the country already has made strides in combating inflation, and its current account gap is starting to narrow.
Inflation should continue in the four percent range this year after slipping to 4.3 percent year-on-year in January, Amnuay said.

He also said his estimate made earlier this year that the current account deficit could narrow to 7.5 percent of gross domestic product in 1997 from around eight percent in 1996 may be too pessimistic.
Amnuay reiterated that the government has announced public spending cuts of 99 billion baht (about US$3.8 billion).
Funding for projects that are low priority, use imported inputs and that are repetitious will lose funding. Military spending also will get the axe, he said.
"But what we will not reduce is development projects," Amnuay said.
The finance minister said the government will set aside funds to improve competitiveness in Thailand's traditional, labour-intensive industries.
Amnuay also said that within the next two months, the government will begin to channel some US$4 billion in provident funds into productive investment, including government and corporate bonds.
Rumours that his economic programme was not supported by the government have no basis in fact, Amnuay said.
"I don't know why there has been some speculation that the finance minister would not get political support. A lot of that is based on imagination," Amnuay said.
"I have got support from the prime minister as well as from the opposition," he added.
Earlier today, Amnuay denied Thai newspaper reports that he planned to resign if his budget cuts were not supported by the government.
